newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese builder may be bid target.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese builder may be bid target.

text.p: Shares of Portugal's biggest construction company Soares da Costa will be volatile in the coming weeks as speculators bet on a takeover bid by a local or Spanish company, analysts said on Friday.

Soares da Costa shares jumped 12 percent to 1,750 escudos ($10.33) on Friday after a brief halt in trade ordered by Lisbon bourse. This followed a newspaper report which said that Portuguese builder Teixeira Duarte might have agreed to buy the company.
Soares da Costa denied the report in Semanario Economico.
"I foresee a speculative frenzy in Soares da Costa. I see volatility but not any sustainable increase in the share price," said one Lisbon-based analyst who asked not to be identified.
Mark Howard of Lloyds Bank Fund Managers in Cascais said he believed a Portuguese company, possibly Teixeira Duarte, or a Spanish group could bid for Soares da Costa.
Another analyst said: "A Spanish or a local group could bid for Soares da Costa, which has not managed its assets well, overloaded its balance sheet with real estate and is over-staffed."

Semanario Economico, which did not reveal its sources, said Fiat Impresit, which controls 25 percent of Soares da Costa, and businessman Salvador Caetano, who controls 20 percent, were unhappy with the performance of their shares.
Soares da Costa stock had failed to keep pace with a buoyant Lisbon bourse as investors penalised the company for its heavy exposure to leveraged real estate projects, analysts said.

They said Teixeira Duarte, a well-managed company active in public works projects including Lisbon's April 25 bridge, had much to gain from purchasing Soares da Costa because the Portuguese construction sector was growing briskly.
The sluggish growth of the Spanish construction market could encourage a Spanish firm to bid for Soares da Costa to take advantage of the brighter prospects in its neighbouring market.
"There is a clear process of concentration going on in the Spanish construction sector," said Juan Simon of Portuguese bank Banco Efisa.
"Economies of scale are better for bigger players, so it would be logical for a Spanish company to look to buy a vulnerable group like Soares da Costa," he said.

Another reason for a possible bid is the possibility that talks between civil engineering group Somague and building firm A.Silva & Silva could lead to the creation of Portugal's biggest construction group.

The two firms announced last month that they had held talks about the possible acquisition by Somague of A.Silva and Silva's building subsidiary Assiconstroi, which is active in private and public sector residential, commercial and industrial building.
"A really big construction company in Portugal would combine synergies and know-how to take full advantage of public works projects where the big margins are for grabs," Howard said.
Soares da Costa shares were at 1,712 escudos, up 152, on volume of 61,116 shares on the Lisbon bourse in the afternoon. ($ = 169.3 Portugese Escudos)
